newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil Congress to focus on oil bill this week.
newsitem.headline: Brazil Congress to focus on oil bill this week.

text.p: A bill opening Brazil's petroleum industry to the private sector is likely to be the highlight of the week in Congress.
A committee in the Chamber of Deputies is expected to vote on the bill Tuesday, and government whips have said they want to put the legislation to a vote on the floor of the lower house Wednesday.
The bill has been delayed on several occasions by arguments over its content, principally a clause which would oblige the government to retain a controlling stake in oil and gas giant Petrobras.
Pro-privatization lawmakers want to eliminate that clause, allowing for a future sell-off of Petrobras, valued at about $20 billion.
The bill regulates a constitutional amendment approved in 1995 by Congress that ended Petrobras' monopoly in several areas of the petroleum industry.
It would allow private companies to compete or enter joint ventures with Petrobras, create a new sector-wide regulator, and end fuel subsidies within three years.
Newspapers Monday said the government wants the oil bill through the Chamber of Deputies this week to allow for a first vote on its civil service reform bill in the week beginning March 17.
As a constitutional amendment, the civil service reform bill has to be approved by two three-fifths majorities in each house.
The Senate was officially scheduled to vote Wednesday on a constitutional amendment that would limit the use of presidential decrees, or MPs as they are known by their Portuguese initials.

MPs are important because they offer the presidency the chance to implement measures quickly, sidestepping often long-winded debate in Congress. Key points of the government's inflation-slashing Real Plan were introduced as MPs in 1994.
But lawmakers resent the power of MPs and have long demanded restrictions on their use. Whips are reportedly negotiating a formula acceptable to both Congress and the presidency.
The government will also have its eye on an ongoing Senate inquiry into an alleged, multi-million dollar fraud involving state and municipal debt.

The probe was due to hear this week officials from state and municipal authorities believed to have underpriced their bonds and from banking and broking executives accused of trading them for quick profits.
